newsitem.title: USA: Missouri leaders optimistic about McDonnell takeover.
newsitem.headline: Missouri leaders optimistic about McDonnell takeover.

text.p: Government and business leaders in Missouri expressed guarded optimism Monday that job losses from the proposed acquisition of McDonnell Douglas Corp. by rival Boeing Co. will be minimal.

"Our mood is cautiously optimistic," said Joe Driskill, director of the Missouri Department of Economic Development. "We believe the defense business of McDonnell Douglas is strong enough that more military business will come their way as a result of the merger."
The company, based in suburban St. Louis, has a sizeable impact on Missouri's economy, with its 23,000 high-wage, high-skilled jobs representing the state's largest private employer.
Driskill said state funds have been used for programs to train workers for the aerospace giant, and that benefit would be extended to the merged company.

While McDonnell Douglas lost out in the potential $200 billion contract to build a new fighter jet, Boeing was named a finalist in the competition and could snare it by gaining control of McDonnell's defense expertise.

"I think the general reaction here is upbeat, combined with some uncertainty," said Murray Weidenbaum, an economist at Washington University in St. Louis and a former chief economist for Boeing. "For the region as a whole, it strengthens the long-term outlook."

McDonnell Douglas' corporate headquarters in Berkeley, a St. Louis suburb, might become te headquarters for the defense segment of the newly merged company, McDonnell spokeswoman Mary Ann Brett said. Boeing headquarters will remain in Seattle.
Brett said the stock-swap merger, valued at $13.3 billion when announced on Sunday, was not expected to result in mass layoffs.
However, analysts said management positions could be cut.

"I would assume over some point in time there will be some attrition in business-related services," said Ed Robb, research director at the University of Missouri's College of Business and Public Administration. "Obviously they're going to lose a couple of people at the top."
The takeover of the region's largest employer could also exact an emotional toll, even though the area remains home to 21 Fortune 1,000 companies.

"McDonnell Douglas has been a model corporate citizen and the hope is that Boeing would continue that traditional role," said David Kemper, president of Commerce Bankshares and chairman of the Greater St. Louis Economic Development Council.
McDonnell Douglas chairman John McDonnell has said he intended to maintain a commitment to St. Louis charities, Brett said.

Ironically, the news of the proposed merger came just as St. Louis County officials were poised to meet with Wall Street rating agencies in the county's quest to have its debt rating raised. On the schedule was a lunch with McDonnell Douglas.

Mitchell Savader, an analyst at Moody's Investors Service, said it was too early to tell what Boeing's takeover of McDonnell Douglas would mean for the county's credit ratings, currently rated Aa1, just a notch below triple-A, the highest rating.
